data.title: Why Bitcoin Just EXPLODED
data.transcript_raw:
Three things happened this month that were each 
supposed to end the crypto rally. The Clarity Act,   the industry's one shot at federal rules, died 
on the Senate floor. The Federal Reserve hiked   interest rates into an already nervous market. 
And the AI trade, the thing soaking up nearly   all the risk appetite in global markets, started 
leaking badly. Each of those was considered the   catalyst that would finally break crypto. And 
yet, Bitcoin decided to ignore all of that and   absolutely rip melting faces on its way to 
$87,000, an 8month high. And over a billion   dollars of positions were wiped out in just 24 
hours, getting it there. So, how does an asset   get handed every single thing it was told to 
fear and go up anyway? Well, to answer that,   we'll break down what actually got liquidated 
overnight, why the worst regulatory news of the   year barely dented the thing it was aimed at, 
and why this dynamic is a great deal older than   this bull cycle. My name is Guy and this is the 
Coin Bureau. So, let's walk through the wall of   worry that Bitcoin just climbed because it's worth 
remembering how bad things looked even just a week   ago. Because last week the Senate held its closure 
vote on the Clarity Act and it failed 49 to 50,   10 votes short of the 60 it needed. That was 2 
years of lobbying with piles of money behind it.   A House bill that had already passed and Clarity 
didn't even get permission to open the debate.   Crypto was heading back to enforcement roulette 
with the regulatory agencies back in charge and   the legislative window was closing ahead of the 
midterms. Coinbase stock fell around 8% that day   and Circle fell about 10%. Then the very next 
day, the Federal Reserve entered the chat with   a unanimous 25 basis point rate hike under new 
chair Kevin Walsh, the first hike since 2023. The   10-year Treasury yield had already spiked above 
5% and the Bank of Japan hiked up to a 31-year   high in the same window. This was the exact macro 
setup that every bare case had been built around.   And on top of all that, the AI trade was taking a 
beating, too. On the 12th of September, Anthropics   Dario Ammedday published an essay arguing the 
industry was moving faster than its own safety   work could handle. And within hours, Sam Alman and 
Elon Musk had both publicly agreed with him, with   Altman then confirming Open AI would not be going 
public this year. By Monday, the semiconductor   index had dropped over 5%, its worst session since 
July. Nvidia and ASML were down hard, and SoftBank   fell almost 11%. So consider all of that mixed 
together from crypto's perspective. clarity's   failure, liquidity tightening, and the risk 
trade that had been carrying the entire market   starting to look weak. If somebody had told you in 
advance that all three of those would land inside   one week, well, nobody's answer for where Bitcoin 
would be trading one week later would be $87,000.   The bears got absolutely everything they asked 
for, but apparently it wasn't enough. Which brings   us to this whopper of a liquidation cascade. As 
I make this video, over the last 24 hours, the   crypto market has seen $1 billion in liquidations. 
And 843 million of those came from shorts. That's   84% of the entire wipeout being driven by 
people who were betting that prices would fall.   Somewhere between 126,000 and 135,000 individual 
accounts were closed out during the sharpest   hour of the breakout. Singlehour liquidations 
crossed $300 million and 97% of that hour was   short positions. So this is really a story about 
two groups of people. One group read all of those   scary headlines I just mentioned and they did 
the obvious thing, positioned for the collapse.   the other group just held. And the billion dollars 
in liquidations belongs almost entirely to that   first group because remember the mechanics behind 
these moves. A short position is a bet that the   price falls. And because traders use leverage and 
only post a fraction of the position's value as   collateral, there is very little room for error. A 
move of just a few% against you is enough to close   a trade. And when the exchange force closes that 
position, it does so by buying. That buying lifts   the price slightly, which trips the liquidation 
level of the next layer of shorts sitting just   above, which forces more buying. Forced buying 
begets more forced buying, which means the rally   that broke those traders was quite literally paid 
for by those traders. Onchain trackers spotted a   single wallet that got liquidated four separate 
times inside 14 hours, losing 375 BTC, around   $32.5 million, doubling down on short after short 
as the thing just kept on climbing. What if you   could trade real US stocks like Apple, Nvidia, or 
Tesla without leaving your crypto account? Well,   that's the idea behind our tokens from BitGet. 
These are tokenized stocks backed onetoone by   real shares, but the key difference is they are 
actually usable. You can trade them, use them as   margin, and even earn dividends instead of just 
letting them sit in your wallet. So, if you want   to check them out for yourself, sign up for BitGet 
using the link in the description or by scanning   this QR code. Now, one important question here is 
why none of that bad news actually stuck. Well,   to answer that, we can first look closer at 
the Clarity Act. Because a bill failing in the   Senate changes only one thing, what politicians in 
Washington have agreed to write down. It doesn't   change whether the network produces blocks or 
whether trading continues on exchanges. It also   doesn't change whether custody works or whether 
crypto users can continue sending peer-to-peer   transactions. Crypto has grown into a trillion 
dollar asset class without regulatory clarity   in the US. Adoption since crypto's inception 
happened within that status quo. And maybe the   funniest part is that the institutions didn't seem 
to get the memo either. Between the 14th and the   20th of September, right through the worst of the 
headline damage, Strategy disclosed buying another   950 BTC for $75 million. US spot Bitcoin ETFs bled 
about $450 million on the day of the vote, the   heaviest single day of redemption since June, and 
then bled a little again the day after. But just   three sessions later, they took in $433 million. 
and Morgan Stanley's Bitcoin ETF has now logged 20   consecutive trading days of net inflows without 
a single down day. Now, none of those desks   care too much about a regulatory bill. They were 
built because the demand was already there. So,   the death of Clarity is really just a story about 
Washington's dysfunction and has little to do with   crypto's actual position in the market. The market 
saw the bill as a nice to have, but when it didn't   get it, it wasn't really all that fussed. Next 
though, we have the macro wall of worry, and this   one is arguably more interesting. The rate hike 
was supposed to be the killer for both traditional   markets and crypto. Bitcoin is a liquidity asset. 
Tighter money means risk assets fall, and crypto   falls hardest of all. That's the thesis. And 
to be fair, there's some solid logic there.   But the market just did something this model says 
shouldn't be possible. Rates went up, yields hit   multi-year highs, the AI complex weakened, and yet 
Bitcoin rallied 13% in 4 days from below 75K. It   also closed its first weekly candle above the 50we 
moving average in 45 weeks. And what's more, total   futures open interest didn't collapse afterwards. 
it actually rose 7.5% to about $156 billion. So,   this clearly isn't just a case of liquidity 
flooding back into the market and dragging Bitcoin   higher with it. There is real demand here. Even 
while some of the usual conditions for a Bitcoin   rally still look pretty ugly, but then again, 
that's not exactly new. Bitcoin has historically   climbed while investors had very good reasons to 
think the whole thing was about to fall apart.   China banned mining back in 2021 and knocked 
more than half the global hash rate offline   as a result. And yet, Bitcoin went from $29,000 
to a new all-time high within just 4 months. FTX   collapsed in November 2022 and took the cycle low 
to $15,400, which turned out to be the absolute   bottom. Three American banks failed in the space 
of a week. In March 2023, USDC briefly lost its   peg and Bitcoin rallied about 40% not long after. 
Now, just for fun, let's look at the mirror image   of that dynamic. Coinbase listed on the NASDAQ 
in April 2021, the most triumphant headline the   industry had arguably ever produced, and it marked 
almost the exact high of that leg. The spot ETFs   were approved in January 2024 after years and 
years of trying, and Bitcoin's price fell from 49K   towards 38K. The moments when everything looked 
good were the tops and the moments when everything   looked terrible were when the gains were truly 
made. So a market that only goes up when the   news is good isn't strong. But a market that goes 
up when the news is uniformly relentlessly bad is   suggesting that there is a pretty strong holder 
base out there. Clarity will likely come back   in some form. The Fed will do whatever the Fed 
does next, and the next round of headlines will   probably be just as convincing as this one was. 
But crypto has already grown to this size through   years of uncertainty and hostility, even some 
moments of outright crisis. Whatever comes next,   though, crypto clearly has a life of its own. But 
what do you think? Are we going higher from here,   or is this one big bull trap waiting to wipe us 
out? Let us know your thoughts in the comments   down below. And if you want to know how to take 
full advantage of this crypto price action,   then you can check out our video on that right 
over here. And by the way, if you're looking for   the best deals in crypto as the market heats up, 
then be sure to check out our deals page. You'll   find the link down in the description or you 
can scan the QR code on screen. Now, as always,   thank you so much for watching and I'll see 
you in the next one. This is Guy signing off.
